questions.q: What is the main point of the article?
options: Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is easy to diagnose with a blood test but has no real treatment
Social media has led many people to claim symptoms of disorders that experts consider mostly imaginary
Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is hard to diagnose but treatable, and patients often find answers online
Hypermobile joints signal a harmless trait, and doctors should stop testing athletes for disorders
questions.explain: The article follows Ivey's long road to an hEDS diagnosis, helped by TikTok, and notes treatments that work.

questions.q: How many people were waiting to be evaluated at Dr. Knight's clinic at last count?
questions.explain: At last count there were 4,000 people waiting at Dr. Knight's clinic.

questions.q: What makes hEDS unusual among the 13 E.D.S. subtypes?
options: It is the only one that is not inherited
It is the only one without a definitive genetic test
It is the only one that affects the skin
It is the only one without symptoms in childhood
questions.explain: hEDS is the only subtype without a definitive genetic test, so diagnosis relies on exams and ruling out other causes.

questions.q: After treatment, what did Ivey estimate her pain level had dropped to?
questions.explain: Her pain had been a 7 out of 10 and is now close to a 3 or 4.

questions.q: What view do the experts quoted take on the online hEDS community?
options: It spreads symptoms through social contagion
It helps people name real, long-standing symptoms
questions.explain: Gensemer says people are finding words for things wrong their whole life, and experts call the contagion idea a misconception.
